newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH ELECTION VIEW-Latest politicians comments.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH ELECTION VIEW-Latest politicians comments.

text.p: The following are the latest comments from French politicians after the first round of voting in France's parliamentary election put the combined left ahead of the ruling centre-right UDF/RPR coalition. The second round is due next Sunday.
PRIME MINISTER ALAIN JUPPE
We want a true change, a change with new ideas, a modern change. And we will do it. French people meant above all to say that they wanted a real change. We must listen to this message.

Real change cannot come from an eccentric coalition of Socialists, Communists, Greens, other leftists, whose programme would put us back 15 years. You can't change by adopting old ideas. To win the second round, the presidential majority...must now mobilise all citizens who want true change
SOCIALIST LEADER LIONEL JOSPIN
I call on all those who want a more balanced government and a new policy for France to unite on this second round.
All those who aspire to change must unite because a change in (the parliamentary) majority is possible and desirable.
I propose to them a pact for change for a new, honest democracy respectful of all and listening to everyone.
The French see their future in the left.
COMMUNIST PARTY LEADER ROBERT HUE
The French people have most vigorously punished the president, his coalition, his prime minister.

I believe that left-wing forces are clearly ahead of the RPR-UDF coalition. It seems to me that the conditions exist for a rallying dynamic to allow a left-wing majority to be elected. The figures are very clear.
I appeal for the broadest rally of left-wing, progressive and ecology forces in favour of the best-placed candidate so that this majority be affirmed.
As for the Communists's performance, there is a slight progress over 1993. It is reinforced and will have more deputies in the National Assembly.
ALAIN MADELIN, FORMER FINANCE MINISTER (UDF)
This is a warning. If we do not take it into account, we will be fired from the classroom. The ruling coalition must clearly show that it has received the message.
CHARLES PASQUA, FORMER INTERIOR MINISTER (RPR)

The French want things to change, they want us to deal more directly with their problems. That will be the issue of the campaign for the second round. The French have the feeling that those in government are too far removed from their concerns. I'm not saying that is true, but that is what the French feel.
FRANCOIS LEOTARD, PRESIDENT OF UDF
We did not win this first round...nothing is decided. The UDF believes that a battle is not won until it is over, and it will be over on June 1 and not before that.
It will do everything so that the prospect for change, its content and guidelines be better presented, proposed and explained within the spirit of freedom that is ours.

The UDF will endeavour to denounce the risk of a takeover by an alliance between the Socialist and Communist parties that is deeply heterogenous and deeply contrary to France's interests in Europe, and to mobilise the citizens in a debate clearly pitting two alliances with deeply different values and orientations."
JACQUES TOUBON, JUSTICE MINISTER
This is not a good result for the current majority. It is a warning shot. It shows some disappointment, irritation, discontent...It will have to be taken into account before the second round.
LAURENT FABIUS, FORMER SOCIALIST PRIME MINISTER

This is a strong rejection of government policy. It think that we have all felt during this camapign the expression of a strong will for change...For the left, it's satisfactory. We will not fall into triumphalism because there is a second round...A change is possible, this evening is perhaps the start of a new hope.
EDUCATION MINISTER FRANCOIS BAYROU (UDF)

The certainty is that the French wanted to send a warning to the government but they don't want a return to the past. The many partisans of the majority who abstained or who spread their votes in the first round will this week mobilise to reaffirm their choice of team for the second round.
NICOLAS SARKOZY, FORMER BUDGET MINISTER (RPR)

You cannot deny these results. I would have liked them to be better. But can the Socialists be happy about these results? The outcome of the vote will be very indecisive, very difficult. We have to explain better what will change on the style of government and the programme to be put in place.
BRUNO MEGRET, DEPUTY LEADER OF THE NATIONAL FRONT

This is a pretty lashing rejection for those who dissolved the National Assembly. It's also an unenthusiastic push for the left, and a very positive result for the National Front...an absolute record that exceeds the score of Jean-Marie Le Pen in the 1995 presidential race.
Asked who he would recommend his supporters to back on the second round, he said: "Candidates of the National Front"
PHILIPPE SEGUIN, NATIONAL ASSEMBLY SPEAKER (RPR)
It is incontestable that the...French people wanted to send us a message. We must now respond to this message, and next Sunday's result will depend on the quality of our response...
As for eventual changes in our team, that concerns only the president and is thus not at stake in the election...

The majority must obviously talk about employment, and thus it must talk about Europe. We are certain now that the battle will be extremely difficult, extremely tense. It is up to us to provide the right reasons.
-- Paris Newsroom +33 1 42 21 53 81
